name: Tarsal tunnel syndrome
aliases: tibial nerve compression at the ankle

reference.source: Green's Operative Hand Surgery / Campbell's Operative Orthopaedics
clinicalPearls: Entrapment of the posterior tibial nerve or its branches beneath the flexor retinaculum (laciniate ligament) behind and below the medial malleolus
Presents with burning pain, paraesthesiae and numbness of the sole and toes, often worse on standing or walking and sometimes nocturnal
A Tinel sign behind the medial malleolus that radiates into the foot supports the diagnosis
The tunnel contents from anterior to posterior are tibialis posterior, flexor digitorum longus, the posterior tibial artery and vein, the tibial nerve and flexor hallucis longus
A space-occupying lesion such as a ganglion, varicosities, lipoma, accessory muscle or tenosynovitis is identifiable in a large proportion of cases
The nerve divides into medial and lateral plantar and calcaneal branches, so symptoms may be confined to part of the sole depending on the branch involved
A dorsiflexion-eversion manoeuvre that tightens the tunnel can reproduce symptoms
Generic management includes orthoses and activity modification, corticosteroid injection, and surgical tarsal tunnel release, especially when a space-occupying lesion is present
reference.pathophysiology: Tarsal tunnel syndrome results from compression of the tibial nerve within the fibro-osseous tunnel behind the medial malleolus, deep to the flexor retinaculum. Raised pressure within this confined space may arise from space-occupying lesions, hindfoot valgus or other deformity, post-traumatic scarring, tenosynovitis or venous engorgement. Sustained compression impairs axonal transport and causes local demyelination, producing sensory disturbance in the plantar distribution and, in advanced cases, weakness and wasting of the intrinsic foot muscles.
additionalDifferentials: Peripheral polyneuropathy, for example diabetic neuropathy
Distal medial plantar nerve entrapment (jogger's foot)
Referred pain or peripheral vascular claudication
additionalInvestigations: Nerve conduction studies and electromyography, recognising that results can be less reliable than at other sites
MRI to identify a space-occupying lesion or accessory muscle within the tunnel
Ultrasound to assess the nerve and surrounding structures dynamically
Weightbearing plain radiographs for bony deformity, coalition or osteophytes
Clinical provocative testing with the Tinel sign and dorsiflexion-eversion manoeuvre
Screening for diabetes mellitus or other systemic causes of neuropathy
redFlags: A mass lesion within the tunnel that may represent a tumour
Rapidly progressive motor loss or intrinsic foot muscle wasting
Features suggesting a systemic neuropathy that requires separate investigation
Evidence of infection or acute trauma around the medial ankle
reference.prognosis: Outcomes are good when a discrete compressive cause such as a ganglion is identified and released, whereas idiopathic cases are less predictable and may have incomplete relief of symptoms.
pitfalls: Confusing the condition with plantar fasciitis or a generalised polyneuropathy and treating the wrong diagnosis
Failing to image the tunnel and missing a space-occupying lesion
Relying on nerve conduction studies, which can be falsely normal, to exclude the diagnosis
Incomplete surgical release that leaves the distal medial and lateral plantar branches decompressed inadequately
management: Excise an identifiable space-occupying lesion such as a ganglion, lipoma, varicosities or accessory muscle, which affords the most reliable outcome
Correct hindfoot deformity and biomechanical factors with orthoses and appropriate footwear
Offer conservative care with activity modification, non-steroidal anti-inflammatory analgesia and neuropathic pain medication
Consider a corticosteroid injection into the tunnel for inflammatory or milder cases
Perform surgical decompression by division of the flexor retinaculum when conservative treatment fails
Screen for and treat diabetes mellitus and other systemic neuropathies contributing to nerve vulnerability
Refer to hand or foot and ankle surgery, counselling that idiopathic cases respond less predictably
